about: Combel-La-Serre is a family estate of about 25 hectares on the limestone plateau, the Causse, above the Lot river, some 17 km from Cahors. The Ilberts have grown grapes here since the early twentieth century but always sold them to the local cooperative. In 1998 Julien Ilbert left the co-op; after several years supplying the négociant Mathieu Cosse, whom he met at a rugby match, he began bottling under his own label in 2005. Julien now runs the estate with his wife, Sophie, and their playful labels and Burgundy-shaped bottles stand out in a traditional region.

The Ilberts work only with Malbec, the historic grape of Cahors, known locally as Côt or Auxerrois. The estate has been certified organic since the 2015 vintage, a change that followed the death of Julien’s grandfather, which the family linked to years of chemical exposure. Au Cerisier comes from a single 40-year-old plot called Rassiels, at 350 metres on red clay over limestone, named for the cherry tree that grows in it. It is fermented traditionally with a maceration of about 25 days, then aged in cement vats only, with no oak, to keep the fruit and the site in focus.

This is a lighter, fresher Cahors than the inky, tannic stereotype. Jancis Robinson’s team praised Au Cerisier for aromatic intensity without overripeness and the structure to age, and the cellar recommends keeping it up to about ten years. Because it never sees oak, the wine’s character comes from the fruit and the plot rather than from barrels. Production is small, about 8,000 bottles a year, and the estate’s distinctive labels make it easy to spot on a list.
